title: The Leningrad Dutch
description: A dynamic defense based on Black's 1...f5 advance, which can be played against d4, c4, and Nf3 by White. Played by many strong Grandmasters, and hundreds of times by Levy.

r1b1qrk1/ppp1p1bp/2np1np1/3P1p2/2P2B2/P1.text: White pushes d5 attacking our knight.

r1b1qrk1/ppp3bp/2np1np1/3Ppp2/2P2B2/P1NB.text: We counterattack the bishop on f4. If White takes en passant, we simply recapture with our bishop, and if White retreats, we have a fork on e4.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/2np1np1/3P1p2/2P2B2/2N.text:
If White pushes d5...

...then we jump into b4 with our knight hitting White's light-squared bishop. 

If they let us take it, we do; if not, we can rotate via a6 to c5.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/2np1np1/5p2/2PP1B2/P1N.text:
White takes away the b4-square from our knight, therefore making d5 more appealing.

A common plan in the Dutch.

We're supporting an ...e5 push and preparing to shift our queen to the kingside in some positions.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/2np2p1/5p1n/2PP1B2/2NB.text:
... then we go after White's dark-squared bishop in order to enable the move ...e5. 

We either capture it on g3 or chase it with ...h6-g5 before capturing it on g3.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/3p1np1/3P1p2/1nP2B2/P1.text:
White attacks our knight.

We trade and win the bishop pair.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/3p1np1/3P1p2/2P2B2/P1N.text:
Forced.

And we plant our knight on a beautiful outpost.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/3p2p1/3P1p2/2P1NB2/P2Q.text:
A blunder!

White thinks that they're winning a pawn, except that we're hiding some nasty plans.

We have to take the knight.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/3p2p1/3P4/2P1QB2/P3PN2.text: White would lose a piece if they don't capture the pawn.

r1bqk2r/pp2p1bp/2np2p1/2p2p2/2PP1B2/2PBP.text: If White plays the natural castles...

r1bqk2r/pp4bp/2np2p1/2p1pp2/2PP1B2/2PBPN.text:
... then we immediately strike in the center with ...e5.

Objectively, this position is close to winning for Black.

r2q1rk1/ppp1p1bp/3p2p1/3P1b2/2P1QB2/P3PN.text:
And we trap the queen!

This is an example of how strong the bishop pair can actually be in an open position.

rnb1qrk1/ppp1p1bp/3p2p1/6B1/2P1N3/3BP3/P.text:
A common idea in the Dutch to shift our queen to the kingside.

Our plans revolve around developing the light-squared bishop to b7, our knight to c5 via a6, and playing ...d6 to control the center without getting in the way of our bishops.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/3p1np1/5p2/2PP1B2/2NBP.text:
White develops and prepares to remove the king from the center.

We develop our knight to c6 inducing White to push d5, giving up the control of e5 and c5.

Even though visually White's position looks promising as all the pieces are developed to some natural squares, White usually doesn't score well as Black here.

rnbqk2r/pp1p3p/6p1/2pP1p2/2P1p3/2P1PN2/P.text:
Connect 4! Eric Rosen would be thrilled to witness this.

We push and force the knight back.

Black is for choice here due to White's bad pawn structure on the queenside.

rnbqk2r/pp1p3p/6p1/2pPpp2/2P5/2P1PN2/P4P.text: White saves the knight and attacks the e5 pawn.

rnbqk2r/pp1pp1bp/6p1/2pP1pN1/2P5/2N1P3/P.text:
White pushes the pawn to gain more space and avoid weakening the pawn structure.

I would rarely recommend trading a fianchettoed bishop for a knight on f3/c3 if it doesn't tactically win.

However, in this case, we're leaving White with 2 weak c-pawns, and an isolated a-pawn, and we can push ...e5 since we would be attacking the White knight.

rnbqk2r/pp1pp2p/6p1/2pP1pN1/2P5/2P1P3/P4.text:
Forced.

Fighting for the center.

White is not in time to take "en passant" since the knight is hanging.

rnbqk2r/pp2p1bp/2pp2p1/4N1B1/Q1PPp3/8/PP.text:
We block the check and the knight is still trapped.

Good game.

rnbqk2r/pp2p1bp/3p2p1/2p2p2/2PP1B2/2PBPN.text:
Forced.

We develop the knight to add more pressure on White's center.

rnbqk2r/pp2p1bp/3p2p1/2p2p2/2PPnB2/2NBPN.text:
Developing and threatening to win a pawn after taking twice on e4.

We take the knight and leave black with doubled c-pawns.

rnbqk2r/ppp1p1bp/3p1np1/5p2/2PP1B2/2N1PN.text:
White connects the pawns and opens up the light-squared bishop's path.

We castle.

rnbqk2r/ppp1p1bp/3p2p1/4N1B1/Q1PPp3/8/PP.text: White delays the problem by checking us.

rnbqk2r/ppp1p1bp/3p2p1/5p2/2PPnB2/2N1PN2.text:
White connects the pawns and opens up the light-squared bishop.

A typical break in these King's Indian-esque structures.

Black wants to soften White's center which will automatically strengthen the bishop on g7.

rnbqk2r/ppp1p1bp/3p2p1/6B1/2P1N3/3BP3/P4.text:
White develops the final minor piece and prepares to castle.

We castle and enjoy having the semi-open f-file for our rook.

rnbqk2r/ppp1p1bp/3p2p1/6B1/2P5/4P3/PPQNP.text: Black could gain a quick initiative if they play aggressively.

rnbqk2r/ppp1p2p/3p2p1/6B1/2P1N3/4P3/Pb3P.text:
While taking the rook is definitely possible, I wouldn't recommend it since Black will have to defend a very unpleasant position due to the weak dark squares.

Instead, Black should focus on catching up with development as we're already up a pawn and we should try to consolidate our advantage.

rnbqk2r/ppp1p2p/3p2p1/8/2P5/4P3/PPQNP1PP.text: Black should catch up in development and the position should be very pleasant to play since we have targets on the e-file.

rnbqk2r/ppppp1bp/5np1/5p2/2PP1B2/2N2N2/P.text:
The 3rd most popular move after 5.Bg5 and 5.e3. 

5.Bf4 has been played in 13% of the games, and White wants to develop the bishop to control the e5-square.

We continue normally with our typical move.

We're covering some important squares in the center and preparing a potential ...e5 or ...c5 push.

rnbqk2r/ppppp1bp/5np1/5pB1/2PP4/2N2N2/PP.text:
This is the most popular move for beginner and intermediate players.

White players opt for 5.Bg5 almost 35% of the time.

A rare sideline in which Black wins 60% of the time!

The idea is to attack the bishop and gain the bishop pair advantage.

rnbqk2r/ppppp1bp/6p1/4N1B1/2PPp3/8/PP2PP.text:
White players might get optimistic and try to move forward with the knight.

We simply attack the trapped knight!

We're controlling every square that the knight can go to.

rnbqk2r/ppppp1bp/6p1/5p2/2PPnB2/2N2N2/PP.text:
Retreating and keeping the bishop.

Preventing any idea of Be5 to trade the bishops.

We will then try to dominate the dark squares in the center and on the queenside with moves like ...c5 and ...Qa5.

rnbqk2r/ppppp1bp/6p1/5pB1/2PPN3/5N2/PP2P.text:
White trades the knight.

We recapture and dislodge the knight from its natural f3 square.

rnbqk2r/ppppp1bp/6p1/5pB1/2PPn3/2N1PN2/P.text:
White might choose to ignore the knight and continue the development.

We take the bishop.

rnbqk2r/ppppp1bp/6p1/5pN1/2PP4/2N1P3/PP3.text:
Forced.

A strategical pawn sacrifice.

7...c5 aims to soften White's center and make our bishop even stronger.

rnbqk2r/ppppp1bp/6p1/6B1/2P1N3/4P3/P4PPP.text:
Opening up the path to developing the light-squared bishop.

Controlling some important squares in the center.

rnbqk2r/ppppp1bp/6p1/6B1/2P5/4P3/PPQNP1P.text:
A risky decision.

White's king could be targeted in the near future.

rnbqk2r/ppppp1bp/6p1/6B1/2PPp3/8/PP1NPPP.text:
White retreats and attacks e4.

This will lead to a sharp line.

We capture on d4 since White blocked the queen's defense over the d4-pawn.

rnbqk2r/ppppp2p/6p1/6B1/2P1N3/4P3/Pb3PPP.text: White sacrifices the rook to win Black's dark-squared bishop which is covering the weak dark squares on the kingside.

rnbqk2r/ppppp2p/6p1/6B1/2P1N3/8/Pb2PPPP/.text:
White saves the rook and attacks our bishop.

We tuck the bishop back on g7 from where it controls the long diagonal.

rnbqk2r/ppppp2p/6p1/6B1/2Pb4/4P3/PPQNP1P.text:
White can take with the pawn to attack the bishop.

We slide the bishop back to g7.

rnbqk2r/ppppp2p/6p1/6B1/2PbN3/8/PP2PPPP/.text:
White takes e4 and opens up and attack on our bishop.

We take one more pawn and attack the rook.

This shows how deadly the bishop on g7 can be once the position opens up.

rnbqk2r/ppppp2p/6p1/6B1/2Pbp3/8/PPQNPPPP.text:
Threatening to capture e4 with the queen.

We're losing the pawn anyways, so might as well damage White's pawn structure while at it.

rnbqk2r/ppppp2p/6p1/8/2Pb4/4B3/PPQNPPPP/.text:
White takes the pawn with the bishop.

We trade bishops and leave White with doubled e-pawns.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5p2/2PP4/2N5/PP2PP.text:
White develops the knight to c3 to fight for e4 71% of the time.

This is where we deviate from all the other setups.

In the Leningrad, we want to fianchetto our dark-squared bishop on g7.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp2p/5np1/5p2/2PP4/2N2N2/PP2.text:
White brings the second knight into the game almost 30% of the time.

Continuing with our plan.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
This is by far the most popular 2nd move.

We develop our knight to f6 from where it will control the e4-square.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Welcome to this course on the Leningrad Dutch!

Well a little spoiler alert, the Leningrad is considered to be one of the most complicated and theoretical variations.

So without further ado, let's dive into the theory.

1r1q1r1k/p1p1p1bp/3p2p1/3B4/2Pn4/4Q3/PP3.text:
We move our king to safety.

I like Black's attacking potential here as all the pieces are developed and active (except the queen) and ...c6 is coming to remove White's strong bishop from the d5-square.

Lest we forget, we also have fork ideas, and b2 is tender.

1r1q1rk1/p1p1p1bp/3p2p1/3B4/2Pn4/4Q3/PP3.text: White retreats the bishop with check.

r1b2rk1/pp1Pp1bp/6p1/2p2p2/1qP5/1Pn1PN2/.text:
White takes on d7 and basically traps our bishop.

We take the d7 pawn since the queen is overloaded and has to keep blocking the discoveries.

r1b2rk1/pp1pp1bp/2P3p1/q1p2p2/2P5/1Pn1PN.text:
White blocks the discoveries and pins our knight.

We move our queen to a square where it's defended in order to be able to move our knight in case White adds a 3rd attacker on it.

r1bq1rk1/p1p3bp/2pp1np1/5p2/2P1B3/2N1PN2.text:
White is losing a piece anyways so might as well win a pawn in the process.

We take back with the pawn attacking the knight.

r1bq1rk1/p1p3bp/2pp1np1/5p2/2P1p3/2N1PN2.text:
White chooses to keep the bishop and give up the knight.

We have to take the piece back.

r1bq1rk1/p1p3bp/2pp1np1/5p2/2P5/2N1PB2/P.text: White recaptures with the bishop and attacks our c6 pawn.

r1bq1rk1/p1p3bp/2pp2p1/8/2PNp1n1/2N1P3/P.text: And now we have a green light to start our kingside assault!

r1bq1rk1/pp1pp1bp/2P3p1/2p2p2/2P1n3/1PN1.text:
White takes our c6-knight.

We take on c3 with the knight.

r1bq1rk1/pp1pp1bp/2P3p1/2p2p2/2P5/1Pn1PN.text:
White saves the queen and adds another attacker on our knight.

We develop the queen adding more defense to our knight and threatening some nasty discoveries on our opponent's king.

r1bq1rk1/pp1pp1bp/2n2np1/2p2p2/2PP4/1PN1.text:
White continues development and prepares to castle.

We connect our pawns and prepare ...e5.

r1bq1rk1/pp1pp1bp/2n2np1/2pP1p2/2P5/1PN1.text:
White pushes the pawn to d5 attacking our knight.

The only move to keep equality!

We have to create a counterattack on White's c3 knight.

r1bq1rk1/pp4bp/2np1np1/2p1pp2/2PP4/1PN1P.text:
And we strike in the center with ...e5!

We successfully achieved what we want from the opening.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/2np1np1/3P1p2/2P5/2N1P.text:
The only critical move!

White attacks our knight and stops ...e5.

This is the main upside of Be2 over Bd3 as ...Nb4 doesn't hit the bishop now.

We go forward with the knight inducing our opponent to create weaknesses on the queenside with a3 and b4 which will open up the long diagonal.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/2np1np1/3P1p2/2P5/2NBP.text:
White pushes the d-pawn to d5 attacking our knight.

We go forward with the knight hitting the light-squared bishop.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/2np1np1/5p2/2PP4/2NBPN.text:
White puts the rook on e1 to prepare an e4 push.

We immediately go for our typical break.

We want to weaken White's center.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/2np1np1/5p2/2PP4/P1NBP.text:
White has 2 main plans in this position:

Playing for an e4 pawn push, and trying to pawn storm the queenside to take as much space as possible.

8.a3 prevents any ...Nb4 ideas and prepares a potential b4 push.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/2np2p1/8/2PPQ3/3B1N2/P.text:
White castles to safety.

We would love to develop our light-squared bishop to g4 and capture the f3-knight, removing one of the defenders of the d4-pawn.

However, the White queen is covering g4, so we develop and force the queen to move and leave the defense of g4 as it has to keep on defending the d3 bishop.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/3p1np1/3P1p2/1nP5/2N1P.text:
White retreats and keeps the bishop pair.

And now we strike in the center with ...e5.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/3p1np1/3P1p2/1nP5/P1N1.text:
White pushes our knight back.

This is the only safe square for the knight.

Even though our knight is kind of misplaced now, it can go back to the center via the c5 square which will be a great square for the knight.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/n2p1np1/3P1p2/1PP5/P1N.text:
White takes more space on the queenside.

A key move!

Whenever our opponent leaves the c3 knight undefended, we have to consider ...Ne4 since we're pinning the knight and attacking it twice.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/n2p2p1/3P1p2/1PP1N3/P3.text: White is forced to sacrifice the exchange now.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1p2p/n2p2p1/3P1p2/1PP1N3/P3P.text: We take the rook. We'll bring the bishop back to g7 and defend against White's knights with h7-h6.

r1bq1rk1/ppp3bp/2Pp1np1/5p2/2P1p3/2NBPN2.text:
White takes the knight.

We're not in a rush to take our piece back since we're forking 2 pieces therefore White cannot save both.

We take back on c6.

r1bq1rk1/ppp3bp/2n2np1/4p3/2P1Pp2/2NB1N2.text:
Keeping the position locked kills the activity of both of White's bishops.

Our plan is to continue development with ...Be6 without getting hit with Ng5.

Therefore, ...h6 is necessary since it prevents Ng5 and prepares ...g5 which could allow us to go for a kingside attack.

r1bq1rk1/ppp3bp/2n2np1/4pp2/2P1P3/2NB1N2.text: White pushes e4 to stop us from playing ...e4.

r1bq1rk1/ppp3bp/2np1np1/3Ppp2/2P5/2NBPN2.text:
White decides to keep the central pawns and pushes d5.

Danger levels!

Tactics will start flowing in the position.

9...e4 forks the bishop and the knight and opens up our dark-squared bishop's diagonal.

r1bq1rk1/ppp3bp/2np1np1/4Pp2/2P5/2NBPN2/.text:
White trades on e5.

We take back with the pawn, threatening a fork with 10...e4.

r1bq1rk1/ppp3bp/2np1np1/4pp2/2PP4/P1NBPN.text:
White will start pawn storming the queenside, so we must react in the center. 

After ...e5, we're threatening a fork with 9...e4 and weakening White's center, which will eventually open up the long diagonal for our dark-squared bishop.

r1bq1rk1/ppp3bp/3pPnp1/5p2/1nP5/2N1PN2/P.text:
White takes en passant.

We take back.

r2q1rk1/pBp1p1bp/3p2p1/8/2Pn4/4Q3/PP3PPP.text:
White wins the b7-pawn.

But this gives our pieces more activity as we have the semi-open b-file for our rook now.

We save our rook with tempo.

r2q1rk1/ppp1p1bp/2np2p1/5b2/2PP4/3BQN2/P.text:
The queen moves and keeps on defending d3 and d4.

The g4-square is undefended now, so we immediately take advantage of this by moving our bishop to g4 attacking one of the defenders of d4.

White doesn't have a good way to save the d-pawn as 12.d5 runs into 12...Bxf3.

r2q1rk1/ppp1p1bp/2np2p1/8/2PP4/4QB2/PP3P.text:
White takes our bishop.

We then take the crucial d4-pawn and plant a strong knight in the center of the board.

The knight on d4 is great compensation for the absence of our bishop pair.

r2q1rk1/ppp1p1bp/2np2p1/8/2PPB1b1/4QN2/P.text:
White makes sure to keep the kingside pawn structure intact at the expense of trading the central d4-pawn for our b7-pawn.

We take the knight.

r2q1rk1/ppp3bp/3pb1p1/5p2/1nP1n3/1PN1PN2.text: ... then we immediately go for ...Ne4 winning material as we're pinning the c3 knight and attacking it twice.

r2q1rk1/ppp3bp/3pbnp1/5p2/1nP5/1PN1PN2/P.text: If White decides to fianchetto the dark-squared bishop on b2...

r4rk1/pp1Qp1bp/6p1/2p2p2/1qP1n3/1P2PN2/P.text:
We move the knight to e4 to cover the d2 square, White cannot block with Qd2 since we can simply take the queen with the knight.

White is simply busted here.

r4rk1/pp1Qp1bp/6p1/2p2p2/1qP5/1Pn1PN2/PB.text:
A huge blunder!

White falls into our trap and takes the bishop.

rnbq1rk1/pp1pp1bp/5np1/2p2p2/2PP4/1PN1PN.text:
White develops the dark-squared bishop to the long diagonal.

We develop the knight to put more pressure on White's center.

rnbq1rk1/pp1pp1bp/5np1/2pP1p2/2P5/1PN1PN.text:
If White pushes the pawn...

... then we move our knight to e4 opening up a double attack on the pinned c3 knight.

rnbq1rk1/pp1pp1bp/6p1/2pP4/2P1p3/1P2PN2/.text:
We take back on e4 attacking both the knight on f3 and the rook on a1.

White is losing material.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/3p1np1/5p2/2PP4/2N1PN2.text:
White castles.

We develop and prepare ...e5.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/3p1np1/5p2/2PP4/2NBPN2.text:
White castles.

We develop the knight to c6 to control the e5 square.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/3p2p1/8/2PPQ3/3B1N2/PP.text:
White develops and prepares to castle.

We develop our knight, putting pressure on White's d4-pawn.

rnbq1rk1/ppppp1bp/5np1/5p2/2PP4/1PN1PN2/.text:
6.b3 was played in 4% of the games in the database that reached this position.

White wants to develop the dark-squared to the long diagonal to challenge our strong bishop on g7.

We immediately try to take advantage of the opening of the long diagonal by pushing ...c5.

rnbq1rk1/ppppp1bp/5np1/5p2/2PP4/2N1PN2/P.text:
6.Be2 has been played 27% of the time.

White develops the bishop timidly to e2 and makes it clear that the plan is not to fight for e4.

We continue with our plan.

We want to prepare our pawn breaks.

rnbq1rk1/ppppp1bp/5np1/5p2/2PP4/2NBPN2/P.text:
By far the most popular move in the position.

White develops the bishop to d3 to start preparing an e4 push in the future.

Our plan will revolve around playing either ...e5 or ...c5 depending on what White plays.

These are our typical pawn breaks in this structure.

rnbq1rk1/ppppp1bp/5np1/5p2/2PPP3/2N2N2/P.text:
White strikes in the center with e4.

We have to take on e4 or else White could push e5 and enjoy a huge powerful center, or they could take on f5 and weaken our pawns. 

The f-pawn hangs and could be safe to take in some lines.

rnbq1rk1/ppppp1bp/5np1/8/2PPN3/5N2/PPQ2P.text:
White takes the pawn back.

We trade knights opening up our dark-squared bishop's scope.

rnbq1rk1/ppppp1bp/6p1/8/2PPQ3/5N2/PP3PPP.text:
Forced.

A typical move in the Leningrad Dutch.

We're preparing to develop our light-squared bishop and to take space in the center with either ...e5 or ...c5 at the right moment.

rnbqk2r/ppppp1bp/5np1/5p2/2PP4/2N1PN2/PP.text:
5.e3 is the 2nd most popular move for White in this position. It's played in 25% of the games that reach this position.

White solidifies the center and prepares to develop the light-squared bishop.

However, this locks the dark-squared bishop behind the f2-d4 pawn chain.

We castle, keeping all options available for our central development.

rnbqk2r/ppppp1bp/5np1/5p2/2PP4/2N2N2/PPQ.text:
A rare but logical move that only occurred in 4% of the games in the database.

White is preparing a quick e4 push trying to weaken Black's kingside.

We castle and prepare to meet e4 with ...fxe4 opening up the f-file for our rook.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5p2/2PP4/2N5/PP2PP.text:
White also starts developing and fighting for the e4 square.

The Leningrad Dutch is on the board! 

We want to fianchetto our dark-squared bishop.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp2p/5np1/5p2/2PP4/2N2N2/PP2.text:
White brings the kingside knight into the game.

We continue with our plan.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White pushes c4 taking space in the center.

We develop our knight control e4.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text: In this study, we'll learn what we should play against 5.e3 and 5.Qc2 using our Leningrad Dutch!

1r1q1rk1/pp2p1bp/3pPnp1/n1p2p2/2P5/2NQ2P.text:
White opened up the long diagonal for the bishop.

However, there's a weakness on e6 now that we can target.

We attack the weak e6-pawn.

1rb1qrk1/1p2p1bp/p2p1np1/n1pP1pN1/2P5/1P.text:
We slide our queen to e8, supporting the b5 push.

...b5 is coming.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
In this study, we'll learn how to counter 5.g3 setups by White when the main 8.d5 push is played.

r1b2rk1/p1p1q1bp/1p1p1np1/n2Ppp2/2P5/1PN.text:
We activate our queen and cover our 7th rank.

The knight will come back to b7 and we'll push ...a5.

Our plans also include a pawn push in the form of either ...e4 or ...f4, or even both, depending on what we want.

r1b2rk1/ppp1q3/3p1bpp/n2Ppp2/2P1P3/1PN2N.text:
We develop our queen to e7 to cover our weak 7th rank.

...b6 is an important move that we have to play soon to create a square for our knight.

r1b2rk1/ppp3q1/6pp/4p3/2PnN3/6P1/PP3PBP/.text:
We retreat to g7, covering our weakened dark squares and the 7th rank.

r1b2rk1/ppp5/2n2qpp/4p3/2P1p3/6P1/PP1N1P.text:

r1bQ1rk1/ppp3bp/2n2np1/4pp2/2P5/2N2NP1/P.text:

White pushes d5, keeping the center closed.

White moves the knight and opens us an attack on our e4-pawn.

White castles.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
In this study, we will continue our exploration of 5.g3 that we saw in the last study. 

This is the strong way in which masters play, but rather than facing the 8.d5 pawn push, we'll explore some alternatives White could play.

1rbr2k1/ppN1p1bp/2n2np1/2p2pB1/2P5/4PN2/.text:
We can just slide the rook to b8 and save it.

The only thing White has achieved here is getting the knight deep into our position.

Now they'll have to waste more moves to get it out.

Meanwhile, we'll develop and enjoy a very comfortable position.

r1b2rk1/ppp2qb1/2n3pp/3NpP2/2P5/3B1N2/PP.text: If White decides to capture on f5, what piece will we recapture with?

r1b2rk1/ppp2qb1/2n4p/3Npp2/2P5/3B1N2/PP3.text:
The pawn!

We want to keep the threat of ...e4 as an option and make White retreat.

r1b2rk1/ppp3b1/2n2qpp/3Npp2/2P1P3/3B1N2/.text:
A more dangerous move is Nd5.

This is the one central weapon White has in these lines that we need to be aware of at all times.

The most common retreating move here is ...Qf7, keeping the queen safe but active.

r1bq1rk1/pp1np1bp/3p1np1/2pP1pB1/2P5/2N1.text:
As we can't develop the knight to c6 now, we'll activate it on d7.

This is good because the knight supports the knight on f6 and we are planning to put a lot of pressure on the g5-bishop now.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/2np1np1/3P1pB1/2P5/2NB.text:
The most critical approach is White pushing d5 here.

What's the best square for our knight?

We'll go for ...Nb4 and target the bishop on d3.

If we could capture it, that would be a great trade for us as it would leave us with the bishop pair.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/2np1np1/5pB1/2PP4/2NBP.text:
Castling allows us to achieve what we wanted the whole time.

We'll grab space in the center.

The threat is ...e4.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/3p1np1/3P1pB1/1nP5/2N1.text:
Retreating to e2 doesn't pose us any problems.

White just succumbed to our pressure and decided to get passive.

To keep the bishop on the active diagonal, White has to play Bb1.

This move does suffocate their rook on a1, as you can see.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/3p2p1/3P1pB1/1nP1n3/2N.text:
We'll go straight for the center, with a similar idea as in the main line.

We've got a lot of pressure on the knight on c3 and on the pawn on b2.

The bishop on g5 is also under attack.

This move allows us to put a lot of pressure on White's knight on c3.

This is where our dark-squared bishop shows its power!

The computer actually suggests White capturing on e4 here and letting us capture on b2 and win the rook.

It's going to be a sharp game either way.

r1bq1rk1/ppp3b1/2n2Bpp/4pp2/2P1P3/2NB1N2.text:
So, White captures.

r1bq1rk1/ppp3bp/2n2np1/4ppB1/2P1P3/2NB1N.text:
That's why White will probably play e4 themselves.

r1bq1rk1/ppp3bp/2np1np1/3PppB1/2P5/2NBPN.text:

r1bq1rk1/ppp3bp/2np1np1/4PpB1/2P5/2NBPN2.text:
Capturing on e5 is just a trade that allows us all the benefits we had before.

We'll take, with the same threat in mind.

r1bq1rk1/ppp3bp/3p1np1/3PppB1/1nP5/2NBPN.text: Once again, we'll go ...Nb4 and attack the bishop on d3. If White moves the bishop, we have ...a5, with a knight reroute to c5.

r1br2k1/pp2p1bp/2n2np1/2p2pB1/2P5/2N1PN2.text:
Let's get the knight out.

As per usual, our main pawn push is ...e5, and there actually isn't much White can do to stop it here.

Going for ...e4 is also good, followed by ...Be6.

rnbQ1rk1/pp2p1bp/5np1/2p2pB1/2P5/2N1PN2/.text:
If White really likes to simplify positions, they'll capture.

A cowardly style of play, if you ask me.

Let's just take back.

rnbq1rk1/pp2p1bp/3p1np1/2P2pB1/2P5/2N1PN.text:
Capturing on c5 leads to some trades but White can't get any advantage.

We'll simply recapture.

Now the queens see each other.

rnbq1rk1/pp2p1bp/3p1np1/2pP1pB1/2P5/2N1P.text:
Grabbing more space and avoiding the trade is definitely a good attempt to confuse us.

However, we're prepared for anything.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/3p1np1/5pB1/2PP4/2N1PN.text:
White could also go for the more passive approach with Be2.

It's important to think of how we'll continue based on what White plays.

When White had the bishop on d3, we played ...Nc6 and ...Nb4. However, there's no bishop on d3 here!

So we won't play ...Nc6 at all. We'll take the opportunity and strike in the center instead.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/3p1np1/5pB1/2PP4/2NBP3.text: If White completely abstains from Nf3...

rnbq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/3p1np1/5pB1/2PP4/2NBPN.text:
White goes for Bd3.

If you see this move, already start to imagine your knight on b4.

You'll see what I mean in a second.

We'll activate the knight to c6, as per usual.

rnbq1rk1/ppp3bp/3p1np1/4ppB1/2PP4/2NBP3/.text:
They've just let us grab a lot of control in the center and achieve ...e5 immediately.

From a positional standpoint, this is great for us.

rnbq1rk1/ppppp1bp/5np1/5pB1/2PP4/2N1PN2/.text:
This move order has not been covered, and White chooses 6.Nf3 around 45% of the time.

In the 2 Knights section, White went 5. Nf3, and we responded with ...Nf6 and ...Ne4.

Now, this is not as good, because White already has e3. White's center is strong.

So we'll just play in normal Leningrad style.

rnbq1rk1/ppppp1bp/5np1/5pB1/2PP4/2NBP3/P.text:
White could also go for Bd3, and they do so 32% of the time.

This could result in a suboptimal setup for them, as you'll see.

We'll go ...d6, with the clear idea of ...e5.

rnbqk2r/ppppp1bp/5np1/5pB1/2PP4/2N1P3/PP.text:
White goes for e3, trying to activate the light-squared bishop.

We will only look at setups without Nf3 here, as mentioned, as those setups were covered in the last chapter.

Having developed the kingside, let's simply castle.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5p2/2PP4/2N5/PP2PP.text:
White develops the knight as well and takes control of some central squares.

The Leningrad Dutch.

We want to fianchetto the dark-squared bishop.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp2p/5np1/5pB1/2PP4/2N5/PP2P.text:
A move played about 27% of the time is Bg5.

Already playing on the dark squares we have weakened around the king, White puts pressure on our knight on f6.

That's okay, as we'll replace those dark squares with our now active bishop.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White goes for the standard approach and places two pawns in the center.

We'll continue as we usually do, activating the knight behind the f-pawn.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
In this chapter, we'll analyze positions after White plays 3.Nc3 and doesn't play 4.Nf3 in our Leningrad Dutch setup.

In this study, we'll cover 4.Bg5 and 4.Bf4 by White.

rnbr2k1/pp2p1bp/5np1/1Np2pB1/2P5/4PN2/PP.text:
If you face Nb5 here, going for Nc7, don't be afraid.

You're completely fine, as there's nothing here.

In fact, you're better, because White is wasting moves on a plan that just doesn't work.

Just remember to get the knight out and free up the b8-square for your rook.

rnbr2k1/pp2p1bp/5np1/2p2pB1/2P5/2N1PN2/P.text:
Instead of going for the pointless Nb5, O-O is more sensible.

We'll continue activating pieces in a standard manner.

r1bqk2r/ppp1p1bp/2np1np1/8/2PPP3/2NB1N2/.text:
White activates their own knight and defends.

How can we put pressure on the defender?

By pinning it to the queen!

r2q1rk1/ppp1p1bp/2np1np1/8/2PPP3/2NBBQ2/.text:
We'll castle, taking advantage of the open f-file.

Our plan is to get the knight to h5 with a discovered attack on White's queen and on the pawn on d4.

Remember to focus on winning that pawn when White gets a pleasant center with three pawns.

r2q1rk1/ppp1p1bp/2np2p1/7n/2PPP3/3BBP2/P.text:
White can defend it by castling, but the semi-open g-file they created might be dangerous for them in the long run.

How can we open up our queen to move towards the kingside?

r2q1rk1/ppp3bp/2np2p1/4p2n/2PPP3/3BBP2/P.text:
By playing ...e5!

We challenge the center and open up the queen at the same time, with the idea of ...Qh4.

If White pushes d5, we can jump our knight into d4.

r2qk2r/ppp1p1bp/2np1np1/8/2PPP1b1/2NBBN2.text:
Adding another defender to the d4-pawn.

Both of the last few moves for both sides were pretty logical.

We'll capture on f3, removing one of the defenders of the d4-pawn.

r2qk2r/ppp1p1bp/2np1np1/8/2PPP3/2NBBP2/P.text:
Capturing with the pawn is bad for White and doesn't change our course of action too much.

We'll still get the knight to h5, with a double attack on the d4-pawn.

There is only one way for White to defend it.

r2qk2r/ppp1p1bp/2np2p1/7n/2PPP3/3BBP2/PP.text:
And that's by bringing the knight back to e2.

There's another pawn in White's camp that's loose, though. And that's f3.

Remember, always look for weaknesses.

And we'll attack it and castle our king at the same time!

r3r1k1/pp4bp/n1p3p1/8/2P5/3B2Pb/PP2NR1P/.text:
The final idea is ...Na6.

We didn't play ...Nd7 because we didn't want to block our rook coming to the d-file.

Also, we want to play ...Nc5 or ...Nb4 with an attack on White's light-squared bishop.

With pressure on most of White's pieces already and more to come, this position is winning for Black!

rn1q1Rk1/pp4bp/2pp2p1/8/2PPB1b1/6P1/PP2N.text:
So they'll most likely capture on f8.

We got what we wanted!

rn1q1rk1/ppp2bbp/3p1np1/3P1p2/1PP1p3/2N1.text:
We'll simply slide back to f7.

White has overextended and has no way forward.

In the meantime, we'll keep developing with ...Qe7 and ...Nd7.

rn1q1rk1/ppp3bp/3pbnp1/3P1p2/1PP1p3/2N1P.text: White's most sensible defense is pushing in the center and attacking the bishop.

rn3qk1/pp4bp/2pp2p1/8/2PPB1b1/6P1/PP2N2P.text:
We'll recapture with the queen.

We already have a very comfortable position and considerable advantage.

What's left is to get the queenside pieces out, probably to d7 and e8.

rnb1r1k1/pp4bp/2p3p1/8/2P5/3B2P1/PP2N2P/.text:
By retreating to d3.

However, we are not done playing with tempo and pressuring White's pieces.

We'll attack White's rook on f1.

rnb2rk1/pp2q1bp/2pp1np1/5p2/2PP1N2/2N1PB.text: We'll simply continue developing, already targeting the e3-pawn.

rnbQ1rk1/ppp3bp/5np1/4pp2/2P5/2N1P1P1/PP.text:
If White really wants to simplify and trade queens, sure.

But the best they can hope for here is a draw.

In many cases, they might actually get a completely lost position.

We'll recapture, of course.

rnbq1rk1/pp2p1bp/2pp1np1/5p2/2PP4/2N3PN/.text:
We'll play ...c6 to take crucial control of the d5-square.

Now neither White's knight nor their bishop can come to the center.

Our main idea is to achieve the ...e5-push.

rnbq1rk1/pp4bp/2p2np1/4pp2/2P5/2N1P1P1/P.text: We'll take control of d5 with ...c6, restricting White's bishop on g2.

rnbq1rk1/pp4bp/2pp1np1/5p2/2PP1N2/2N1PBP.text:
In the absence of our pawn on e5, White can afford to play Nf4.

But the d5-square is untouchable for the moment.

rnbq1rk1/pp4bp/2pp1np1/5p2/2PPP3/2N2BP1/.text:
If White goes for the more challenging e4, playing in the center, they might be too ambitious.

We'll capture with the knight, forcing some trades.

rnbq1rk1/pp4bp/2pp2p1/5p2/2PPN3/5BP1/PP2.text:
Once White recaptures...

Now the pawn arrives on e4, forcing White to capture again.

rnbq1rk1/pp4bp/2pp2p1/8/2PPB3/6P1/PP2N2P.text:
Which they will.

Trading rooks on the f-file would just get White's queen there.

We would rather they capture our rook on f8.

So we'll play ...Bg4, pinning the knight to the queen.

White can't play Bf3 back, as the bishop would be hanging.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/3p1np1/5p2/2PP4/2N1P1P.text:
The knight develops to e2 instead of f3.

The idea is not to block the bishop and maintain pressure on the b7-pawn, and to jump to f4 in some lines.

We'll put our ...e5-push into motion.

There is actually another idea behind ...e5 that we don't see in the other lines!

rnbq1rk1/ppp3bp/3p1np1/4Pp2/2P5/2N1P1P1/.text:
If White decides to capture immediately, that doesn't bother us.

We'll still get a strong center.

Let's simply take back.

rnbq1rk1/ppp3bp/3p1np1/4pp2/2PP4/2N1P1P1.text:
Avoiding the center trade and castling is probably better for White.

And here's the other idea of ...e5.

We actually push the pawn to e4, completely blocking White's bishop on g2 and closing the center!

We've suddenly grabbed a lot of space, and White probably won't let the position remain like this for long.

rnbq1rk1/ppp3bp/3p1np1/4pp2/2PP4/2NBP3/P.text:
And believe it or not, after 7 moves, Black is better!

This way of playing is far from the best for White.

The bishop on c1 is still at home, and we could argue that the knight on e2 is misplaced.

rnbq1rk1/ppp3bp/3p1np1/5p2/1PPPp3/2N1P1P.text:
Instead of dealing with the center, White might completely give up on it and play on the queenside.

We'll immediately attack the c4-pawn, which now can't be defended with b3.

Remember, every pawn push changes something in the position!

Sometimes that something is more important than it looks.

rnbq1rk1/ppp3bp/3p1np1/5p2/2PP4/2N1PBP1/.text:
White recaptures with the bishop.

Anytime the bishop is free in the middlegame, a move should come to your mind.

It's ...c6.

rnbq1rk1/ppp3bp/3p1np1/5p2/2PPp3/2N1PPP1.text:
Expect your e4-pawn to be challenged immediately.

I recommend taking here.

White has weakened the e3-pawn and we'll still keep a pawn chain on the kingside.

rnbq1rk1/ppp3bp/5np1/4pp2/2P5/2N1P1P1/PP.text: If White castles, remember the defensive move we usually play in the 4.g3 lines.

rnbq1rk1/ppppp1bp/5np1/5p2/2PP4/2N1P1P1/.text:
After playing g3, it's common for White to block the bishop on c1 with e3.

The bishop doesn't have many active squares to develop to and can get kicked around easily.

That's why White saves its development for later.

We'll continue with our setup, aiming for ...e5.

rnbq1rk1/ppppp1bp/5np1/5p2/2PP4/2N3PN/PP.text:
Nh3 is a developing possibilty for White if they don't want to block their light-squared bishop and quickly castle.

We'll continue normally, opening up our light-squared bishop.

Our idea is still to play ...e5 at some point, regardless of White's developing setup.

rnbq1rk1/ppppp1bp/5np1/5p2/2PP4/2NBP3/PP.text:
If White really wants to avoid the 2 Knights positions, they'll develop the g-knight to e2 instead of f3.

However, this doesn't provide them any benefits.

We'll just keep developing.

The ...d6-push opens up the light-squared bishop and prepares ...e5.

White doesn't have a knight on f3, so they can't really stop our advancement.

rnbqk2r/ppp1p1bp/3p1np1/5p2/2PPP3/2NB1P2.text:
White activates the bishop to add more protection to the e4-square.

Now exf5 might be unpleasant as we would have to recapture with the g-pawn at some point and weaken our kingside.

So we'll capture in the center.

rnbqk2r/ppp1p1bp/3p1np1/8/2PPP3/2NB4/PP4.text:
White recaptures with the pawn, maintaining a strong center.

Our forces should now move towards attacking the d4-pawn, as it is the only undefended one and the one hardest to defend.

If we can win it, we'll be in great shape.

So we'll develop the knight, targeting the d4-pawn.

rnbqk2r/ppppp1bp/5np1/5p2/2PP4/2N3P1/PP2.text:
White goes for the fianchetto as well.

We remain with our setup.

Having developed all the kingside, we'll castle.

rnbqk2r/ppppp1bp/5np1/5p2/2PP4/2NBP3/PP3.text:
The bishop gets out to the most active d3-square.

As our kingside is developed, we'll castle, bringing the king to safety.

rnbqk2r/ppppp1bp/5np1/5p2/2PPP3/2N2P2/PP.text:
White will continue with their plan, getting a big center.

Capturing on e4 here justifies White's bad setup, so we won't do that just yet.

We'll take control of the e5-square.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5p2/2PP4/2N5/PP2PP.text:
The three most standard opening moves we've seen many times throughout this course.

Let's go for the Leningrad Dutch.

We want to fianchetto the dark-squared bishop and go for a sharp setup.

From here on, we'll cover White's three options: 4.e3, 4.f3 and 4.g3.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp2p/5np1/5p2/2PP4/2N1P3/PP3.text:
As in some of the previous chapters we've seen, 4.e3 is not really a logical move, because it blocks the dark-squared bishop.

Hence, it is played only 11% of the time.

Our setup shouldn't change as White hasn't challenged us in any way.

They've only crippled themselves.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp2p/5np1/5p2/2PP4/2N2P2/PP2.text:
Going for 4.f3 is something I really assume you won't be getting a lot in your games, although it's played about 10% of the time in the Masters database.

The idea is simple: e4.

There's not much we can do to prevent e4 right away, so we'll just keep activating pieces.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp2p/5np1/5p2/2PP4/2N3P1/PP2.text:
4.g3 is actually the most popular fourth move in high-level games, played about 40% of the time!

It is definitely a decent setup with the bishop on g2, and one that basically forces us to play ...c6 at some point, which is already a downgrade from ...Nc6.

However, White playing like this allows us to get an easy ...e5, which is definitely what we want.

We'll keep developing ourselves.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
Grabbing space in the center.

We'll build behind the pawn, as per usual.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
In the second study of this Chapter, we'll take a look at three other options for White on move 4, all of them having their own advantages and disadvantages in the Leningrad Dutch.

Let's dive right into it!

rnbr2k1/pp4bp/2p2np1/5p2/2P1P3/2N2BP1/PP.text:
White might want to get rid of their weakness of e3 and open up their bishop.

We'll take in the center.

rnbr2k1/pp4bp/2p2np1/8/2P1N3/5BP1/PP2N2P.text:
Once White recaptures, trading again helps us open up our bishop and go after White's misplaced pieces.

So we'll do that.

rnbr2k1/pp4bp/2p3p1/8/2P1B3/6P1/PP2N2P/R.text:
Natural.

What move do we have here that skewers two pieces?

We bring the rook to the e-file.

Lucky for them, White can defend both the bishop and the knight...

rnbr2k1/ppp3bp/5np1/4pp2/2P5/2N1P1P1/PP2.text:
If White castles, there's a great positional move we can play.

We grab more space in the center, limit White's bishop and open up our own!

rnbr2k1/ppp3bp/5np1/5p2/2P1p3/2N1PPP1/PP.text:
If White doesn't like our pawn chain and wants to break it apart instantly, they are already walking into dangerous waters.

The e3-pawn is already much weaker.

We'll take, as letting White capture would weaken our position too much.

rnbr2k1/ppp3bp/5np1/5p2/2P5/2N1PBP1/PP2N.text:
White recaptures with the bishop.

We'll take control of d5 once again, before going after White's weaknesses.

rnbq1rk1/pp4bp/2pp1np1/5p2/2PPp3/1P4P1/P.text: And now we try to push ...d5 to claim a nice central control.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/3p1np1/5p2/2PP4/1P3NP1.text:
White prepares to fianchetto their other bishop.

Let's grab some space in the center!

We've pushed ...d6, so playing ...e5 is only logical.

Looks like White is covering the e5-square well, but thanks to the open dark-squared diagonal, we have some tactical opportunities.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/3p1np1/5p2/2PP4/2N2NP1.text:
Most of the time, players will go for 
7. Nc3, transposing into the 2 Knights chapter with g3. 

Nonetheless, we'll first go ...Nc6.

Let's look at some other sidelines.

rnbq1rk1/ppp3bp/3p1np1/4Pp2/2P5/1P3NP1/P.text:
White goes ahead and captures on e5.

We simply recapture.

rnbq1rk1/ppp3bp/3p1np1/4pp2/2PP4/1P3NP1/.text:
White may opt for a queenside fianchetto.

We'll close down the center and occupy some light-squares.

rnbq1rk1/ppp3bp/6p1/4Np2/2P3n1/1P4P1/P3P.text:
The dark-squared bishop is now active on the diagonal, and we put pressure on White's e5-knight.

The computer suggests that White capture the knight on g4 and give up the rook, claiming a slight advantage for Black.

rnbq1rk1/ppppp1bp/5np1/5p2/2PP4/5NP1/PP2.text:
White also castles.

We're going for the Leningrad Dutch!

This move is played to control some central squares while opening up the light-squared bishop and preparing to push ...e5.

rnbqk2r/ppppp1bp/5np1/5p2/2PP4/5NP1/PP2P.text:
White develops the bishop.

Let's simply get the king out of the center!

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5p2/2PP4/5N2/PP2PP.text:
White brings their kingside knight out to f3 11% of the time.

The least challenging approach from White.

We prepare to fianchetto the dark-squared bishop.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp2p/5np1/5p2/2PP4/5NP1/PP2P.text:
White does the same. 

Our opponent opted for a Catalan setup, characterized by a light-squared bishop fianchetto and by the d and c-pawns covering some central squares.

Expect to see this move 16% of the time.

We respond traditionally, by bringing the dark-squared bishop on a strong diagonal.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White continues to advance their pawns.

We develop a piece while adding control to the e4-square.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text: In this study, we'll look at a Catalan setup with 4. g3, which White could go for after 3. Nf3.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/2np1np1/3P1p2/2P2B2/3B.text:
The move d5 looks enticing, so White goes ahead and attacks our knight.

We'll attack the bishop now.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/2np1np1/5p2/2PP1B2/4PN.text:
We play very similarly even if White goes for 6. Be2. 

...e5 coming!

r1bq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/2np2p1/5p2/2PPnB2/3BPN.text:
The knight jumps out to c6.

Once again, the plan is pushing ...e5 and getting some piece activity. 

White is yet to develop their b1-knight, as opposed to our very strongly placed knight on e4.

r1bq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/3p2p1/3P1p2/1nP1nB2/4P.text:
The knight gets centralized. 

We have some nice-looking, active pieces, all green, of course.

Another plan is to push ...c6 and pressure White's central structure.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/3p1np1/5p1P/2PP1B2/4PN.text:
White continues the attack.

Let's call White's bluff! 

This attack will most likely fail.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/3p1np1/5p2/2PP1B1P/2N1.text: We can expect development from White.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/3p1np1/5p2/2PP1B2/3BPN.text:
White castles.

A nice square for the knight. 

It supports the e5-pawn push, and aims at the b4-square.

This is just a transposition into the two Knights chapter, without White playing Nc3.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/3p2p1/5p1R/2PP1B2/4PN2.text:
White's intentions are to sacrifice the exchange.

We'll recapture it, no worries.

rnbq1rk1/ppp1p1bp/3p4/5pNp/2PP1B2/4P3/PP.text:
White opens up their queen.

Since the action is happening on the kingside and White's king is uncastled, it's now a good time to strike in the center!

rnbq1rk1/ppp3b1/3p3p/4ppNQ/2PP1B2/4P3/PP.text:
White has two pieces under attack, their king is still in the center and our pieces will get activated quickly. 

We'll take the win shortly.

rnbq1rk1/ppp3bp/3p4/4ppNQ/2PP1B2/4P3/PP3.text: Checkmate is threatened but It's quite easy to stop this attack.

rnbq1rk1/ppp3bp/3ppnp1/5p2/2PP1B1P/2N1PN.text:
A solid response. Let's cover some central squares! 

We'll develop the knight to c6 first and eventually push ...e5 with the support of our queen on e7.

rnbq1rk1/ppppp1bp/5np1/5p2/2PP1B1P/4PN2/.text:
White tries to be annoying with computer moves, but this move isn't played very often.

We continue with our plan in the Leningrad Dutch.

rnbq1rk1/ppppp1bp/5np1/5p2/2PP1B2/3BPN2/.text:
White is developing.

Habitually, ...d6 should be played.

rnbq1rk1/ppppp1bp/5np1/5p2/2PP1B2/4PN2/P.text:
White chooses a more conservative approach.

We'll play ...d6, as per usual.

rnbqk2r/ppp1p1bp/3p2p1/5p2/2PPnB2/3BPN2/.text:
White develops and puts pressure on our knight.

Let's waste no time and get castled quickly!

rnbqk2r/ppppp1bp/5np1/5p2/2PP1B2/4PN2/PP.text:
White prepares to develop their bishop.

We hide our king on the kingside.

rnbqk2r/ppppp1bp/6p1/5p2/2PPnB2/4PN2/PP3.text:
White solidifies the center and opens up the light-squared bishop.

As per usual, we open up the light-squared bishop and prepare the ...e5-push.

rnbqk2r/ppppp1bp/6p1/5pB1/2PPn3/2N2N2/PP.text:
...but this just transposes into the previous chapter.

Let's look at something different.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp1pp/5n2/5p2/2PP4/5N2/PP2PP.text:
White is also beginning to develop.

Of course, we prepare to fianchetto the dark-squared bishop.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp2p/5np1/5p2/2PP1B2/5N2/PP2.text:
Another move that White could go for is Bf4 immediately.

However, it's only played 3% of the time.

...Ne4 now would be a bit too premature, since it doesn't come with an attack on anything and White simply develops next.

Very standard development for our bishop.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp2p/5np1/5pB1/2PP4/5N2/PP2P.text:
White immediately brings their bishop to g5 9% of the time.

Now we simply centralize our knight and put pressure on White's g5-bishop.

rnbqkb1r/ppppp2p/6p1/5p2/2PPnB2/5N2/PP2P.text:
White retreats to f4.

We respond with development and prepare to castle.

rnbqkbnr/ppppp1pp/8/5p2/2PP4/8/PP2PPPP/R.text:
White brings out their d- and c-pawns.

We start to develop the kingside pieces.

rnbqkbnr/pppppppp/8/8/3P4/8/PPP1PPPP/RNB.text:
Instead of 4. g3, White could choose to go for some other moves with the dark-squared bishop.

This study will cover them!
